# Wobble Rush 3D — Design Reference Report

Research for an **original** Fall-Guys-style 3D obstacle-course time-trial. No Fall Guys assets, character designs, or trademarks are recommended; the two "clone" repos below are cited **only** as tuning-value references (their shipped `fall-guy-base-rig` art assets are unlicensed rips and must not be used — see warning in §5).

**Sourcing honesty:** Every URL below was fetched this turn. Where a claim is a *recommendation derived from* a source rather than quoted from it, I label it **[inference]**. GDC talk transcripts could not be retrieved (Game Developer / GDC Vault pages exceeded the read-only fetch buffer and several are login-walled) — see the flagged note in §1.

---

## 1. Obstacle-course level-design principles (physics-party games)

**Core principle — progressive difficulty & safe spacing.** Wikipedia's level-design article states levels "generally have progressively increasing difficulty to appeal to players with different skill levels" and "may present new concepts and challenges to keep a player's interest." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_(video_games))

**Genre context.** *Fall Guys* is a "free-to-play platform battle royale" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_Guys); sibling physics-party games *Gang Beasts* (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gang_Beasts) and *Human: Fall Flat* (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human:_Fall_Flat) establish the bumbling-physics-runner vocabulary. The TV format that originated the "gauntlet of wipeout obstacles" archetype is *Wipeout*, "contestants competing in the 'World's Largest' obstacle course" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wipeout_(2008_game_show)).

**Concrete pacing heuristics [inference from player physics in §2]:** With the reference player moving at **5 m/s** (see §2, PlayerMove_LJH `speed = 5`), a 60–90 s course is ~300–450 m of path length. Practical density budget for a fair-but-frantic course:
- **Obstacle spacing:** one discrete obstacle every ~8–14 m of forward travel (≈1.6–2.8 s at 5 m/s) so the player has time to read the next hazard before committing.
- **Safe-zone breathing room:** a flat "rest" pad of ≥4 m (~0.8 s) between any two moving hazards, larger (≥8 m) after a section that can knock the player down (dive/getup state adds recovery time).
- **Checkpoint placement:** place a respawn checkpoint immediately after every "knockdown-capable" hazard (sweepers, spinners, bumps) and at every ≥6 m fall-risk gap, so a failure costs ≤3–5 s rather than a full-section redo. The LeeHaEun1 clone ships `RespawnCheck_LJH.cs` + `RespawnCheckCube`/`RespawnCheckCylinder` prefabs exactly for this pattern (repo tree: https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/tree/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Resources/Prefabs/Prefabs_LJH).
- **Readability / telegraphing:** moving hazards should begin a visible motion cycle ≥0.6 s before the player's earliest possible arrival at the contact zone (the LightRod example uses a 2 s dwell at each end — §2 — which doubles as the telegraph window).
- **Difficulty ramp for 60–90 s:** ~3 beats — (a) intro 0–25 s: single static/moving hazard per segment, wide lanes; (b) mid 25–65 s: compounded hazards (moving platform **plus** sweeper), narrowing lanes; (c) finale 65–90 s: a single high-stakes "money shot" obstacle (long jumping gap or fast spinner) feeding directly into the finish line.

**⚠ Flag — GDC talks not retrieved.** Specific GDC Level Design Workshop transcripts (gdcvault.com) and Game Developer long-form articles could not be fetched this turn (read-only `curl` returned a buffer-size error on those large pages; GDC Vault is also login-gated). The principles above are therefore anchored on the Wikipedia level-design article plus the primary-source implementations in §2, **not** on a quoted GDC talk. Treat any later "GDC says X" claim as unverifiable until a transcript is retrieved.

---

## 2. Obstacle archetypes & concrete tuning

All numbers below are read directly from source at the cited permalinks. Values are in engine units (Unity = meters; Unreal = cm).

### Rotating sweeper bars
`BeamRotate_LHE` spins around the up-axis at **`speed = 150` deg/s** (≈ **25 RPM**); `BladeRotate_LHE` spins a blade around forward-axis at the same **150 deg/s**. The blade script's comment notes the contact design: on arm–player collision the arm's anchor rotation is set non-kinematic so real physics imparts the knock. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LHE/BeamRotate_LHE.cs#L7-L19 and https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LHE/BladeRotate_LHE.cs#L7-L19)

**Clear-height guidance [inference from player jump physics]:** the reference player jumps with `jumpPower = 5` (Unity units/s upward) under default gravity, giving an apex height ≈ v²/(2g) = 25/19.62 ≈ **1.27 m** (player physics: https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/PlayerMove_LJH.cs#L10-L18). So a horizontal sweeper bar the player must jump **over** should sit with its underside at ~0.4–0.7 m above the floor (clears with margin); a bar the player must **duck/pass under** (if you add a slide) sits at ~1.6–1.8 m. Arm length 2–3 m is typical so the swept arc covers most of a ~3–4 m wide lane but leaves a readable timing gap.

### Moving platforms (travel time, dwell, carrying the player)
`AMovingPlatform` (Unreal, UE units = cm) defaults to **`PlatformVelocity = (100,0,0)`** (100 cm/s = **1 m/s**) and **`MoveDistance = 100`** (1 m), reversing when `GetDistanceMoved() > MoveDistance`. That yields **~1 s travel each way, ~2 s full cycle**, with no programmed dwell. (https://github.com/james-truong/FallGuysClone/blob/e1eeec22e829faee846421d29dd25e081edbc314/Source/ObstacleAssault/MovingPlatform.h#L27-L31 and https://github.com/james-truong/FallGuysClone/blob/e1eeec22e829faee846421d29dd25e081edbc314/Source/ObstacleAssault/MovingPlatform.cpp#L36-L51)

**Carrying the player — concrete pattern:** the clone's conveyor `ConveyorBelt_LJH` carries riders by directly translating their transform along `transform.forward * speed * deltaTime` and freezing X/Z rotation while on the belt (restored to `None` on exit). This is the robust way to make a kinematic platform "carry" a physics character. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/Obstacles/ConveyorBelt_LJH.cs#L20-L33) **[inference]** for rideable platforms that aren't belts, parent-or-velocity-transfer with ~0.4–0.8 m/s carry speed reads as "fair and rideable"; faster than the player's 5 m/s run is unfair.

### Bouncing bumpers (impulse response)
`Bumper_LJH` and `SpinningBlade_LJH` implement the bumper not as an additive impulse but by **swapping the player's PhysicMaterial `bounciness`** on contact (to a per-bumper `bounciness` value) and restoring a **default of `0.2f`** on exit. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/Obstacles/Bumper_LJH.cs#L21-L37 and https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/Obstacles/SpinningBlade_LJH.cs) **[inference]** `bounciness` ∈ [0,1] in Unity maps to coefficient of restitution; 0.2 = mild, 0.6–0.8 = strong arcade pop, 1.0 = perfectly elastic (avoid — unstable). Tune the bumper's restitution to ~0.55–0.7 and add a small additive normal impulse on contact for a "boing" that's readable but never launches the player off-course unpredictably.

### Vertical piston / drop rod (rhythm telegraph)
`LightRod_LJH` is a vertical piston cycling between Up/Down positions at **`speed = 0.5f`** (0.5 m/s) with **`waitTime = 2f`** (2 s dwell at each end), polling motion at 10 ms cadence. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/Obstacles/LightRod_LJH.cs#L12-L14) This 2 s dwell is a good baseline for the "telegraph window" called for in §1.

### Narrow bridges (width relative to character radius)
No source provided an explicit bridge-width constant. **[inference]** the player uses a `BoxCollider` (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH/PlayerMove_LJH.cs#L19-L20); a chunky bean-style body is roughly 0.5–0.6 m wide. Bridge-width tuning that reads as "tense but fair": **≈2.5–3× body width ≈ 1.3–1.8 m**. Below ~2× width the course feels punishing; above ~4× it stops registering as a hazard.

---

## 3. Bright, toy-like 3D art direction

**Color-theory foundation.** Wikipedia: "Color theory … describes the behavior of colors — namely in color mixing, color contrast effects, color harmony, color schemes and color symbolism." (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_theory) For a toy-like racer this means: **saturated primaries** for hazard/interactive elements, **candy pastels** for safe geometry, and **deliberate value contrast** so hazards pop against floors.

**Vinyl/plastic material archetype — real reference.** Epic's stock UE Mannequin material-layer kit (shipped free with the engine, present in the james-truong tree) ships exactly the surface types a toy aesthetic wants: `ML_Plastic_Shiny_Beige`, `ML_GlossyBlack_Latex_UE4`, `ML_SoftMetal_UE4` (https://github.com/james-truong/FallGuysClone/tree/e1eeec22e829faee846421d29dd25e081edbc314/Content/SCK_Casual01/Mannequin/Character/Materials/MaterialLayers). Use these as the *archetype* (plastic-shiny base, glossy-latex accent, soft-metal hardware) — rebuild originals, don't import the `.uasset` files.

**Art-direction rules [inference from the above]:**
- **Hazard vs safe by value, not just hue:** keep hazard surfaces 1.5–2 stops **darker or more saturated** than adjacent safe floors so a player reads danger in peripheral vision.
- **One material family:** everything reads as vinyl/plastic → low roughness variance (0.15–0.35), moderate specular, no real-world grime. Metal only on fasteners/hinges.
- **Background/skybox:** desaturated candy gradient (e.g. soft lilac→peach) so saturated foreground geometry pops; bake soft clouds as flat cards, avoid high-frequency skybox detail that competes with hazards.

**Original hex palettes (my recommendations, derived from color-theory principles above — NOT Fall Guys' palette):**

| # | Use | Hex |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | Primary course / safe floor | `#7FD8FF` (sky plastic) |
| P2 | Secondary platform | `#FFD66B` (banana yellow) |
| P3 | Accent / collectible | `#FF6B9D` (bubblegum pink) |
| H1 | Hazard (sweeper/spinner) | `#FF4D4D` (toy red) |
| H2 | Hazard highlight stripe | `#FFD400` (caution yellow) |
| S1 | Safe "rest" pad | `#A8E6A1` (mint) |
| S2 | Border / guard rail | `#3A4A7A` (toy navy) |
| BG1 | Skybox top | `#C9B6FF` (lilac) |
| BG2 | Skybox horizon | `#FFD9C0` (peach) |
| INK | Silhouette / outline | `#2B2D42` (near-black navy) |

These are constructed (saturated primaries P1–P3, candy pastels S1/BG1/BG2, dark INK for readable silhouettes) and are **original to Wobble Rush 3D**.

---

## 4. UI/HUD conventions for arcade time-trial racers

**Genre conventions.** A time trial is "a race … against the clock to secure the fastest time," each starter released "at a predetermined interval" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_trial). *TrackMania* is the canonical build-your-own arcade racer where tracks are "saved as 3D files" and replays/time are central (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TrackMania); *Mario Kart* defines the minimal, high-readability kart HUD convention (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario_Kart).

**Concrete timer implementation — fetched.** The LeeHaEun1 clone's `Timer_merged` shows a real, shippable pattern: a **countdown** from `limitTime = 180` (s), rendered as **`(int)limitTime/60 + " : " + Mathf.Round(limitTime%60)`** (i.e. `M : SS`), decremented one displayed second per `timeMultiplier` (50) fixed frames, with a `failImage` shown and a result scene loaded on timeout. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/blob/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LHE/Timer_merged.cs#L11-L24)

**Recommendations for Wobble Rush 3D's *time-trial* HUD [inference]:**
- **Timer format:** for a *time-trial stopwatch* (not the clone's countdown) use **`MM:SS.mmm`** (millisecond precision) — the genre standard for "fastest time" framing. Keep the timer top-center, large, monospaced; show `Δ` to best-lap in a smaller secondary color (green if ahead, red if behind).
- **Checkpoint indicator:** a minimal "CP 2/5" pip row along the top, lighting each pip on pass; a split-time popup (`−0.342`) that fades in ~0.8 s.
- **Minimal HUD:** only timer, checkpoint pips, and (optionally) a small speed/coin counter bottom corners. No minimap for a 60–90 s linear course — the track is the map.
- **Start screen:** 3-2-1-GO countdown overlay with the course name and best time; gate player input until GO. **Finish screen:** large final time, "NEW BEST!" stamp if applicable, lap/split breakdown, and `Retry` / `Next` buttons. The clone has matching `StartUIManager_LJH.cs` + `ShowResult_LJH.cs` modules (repo tree: https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/tree/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Scripts/Scripts_LJH).

---

## 5. Original character design — chunky rounded runner (NOT Fall Guys)

**⚠ IP warning (verified).** The LeeHaEun1 clone ships an unlicensed `Assets/Resources/Resources_LJH/Character_lJH/fall-guy-base-rig/` folder containing `FallGuy_BaseColor.png`, `fallGuyBase.fbx`, etc. (https://github.com/LeeHaEun1/FallGuys_Clone/tree/1339106e53dd47ea0a11149b16d2509027173425/Assets/Resources/Resources_LJH/Character_lJH/fall-guy-base-rig). **Do not use these.** They are ripped Fall Guys assets. Use only the *code tuning values* from these repos; design Wobble Rush's mascot from scratch per the direction below.

**Conceptual anchor.** A mascot is "anything used to represent a group with a common public identity … also used as fictional, representative spokespeople for consumer products" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mascot); characterization is "the art of creating characters" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Character_(arts)).

**Original direction for the "Wobble" runner [inference / design recommendation — derived from mascot & shape-language principles, not a specific cited source]:**
- **Shape language — distinctly NOT the bean.** Fall Guys is a near-spherical capsule with a face on the front. Differentiate Wobble via a **stacked, slightly pear/tadpole silhouette**: a large rounded-egg **body** sitting on **two stubby cylindrical legs** (no arms, or vestigial nubs), capped by a **small dome "head"** that is *part of* the body rather than a separate sphere. Read as a "wobbling top / weeble," not a bean.
- **Proportion ratios (body-height units):** total height ≈ 1.6 body-widths (chunky); head-dome ≈ 0.35 of body height and centered low; legs ≈ 0.18 of total height; feet wider than legs (flare out) for a stable, toy-like stance. Center of mass visibly low (bottom 40% of silhouette) → reinforces the "always rights itself" wobble read.
- **Color-blocking:** two-tone — a saturated body color (use P1–P3 from §3) with a contrasting **belly panel** (S1) on the lower front; a single accent stripe or cap color (H2) on the dome. Avoid face-on-front duplication of the Fall Guys look: put **two simple eye dots high on the dome** and a small smile, or go **faceless** with an expressive tilt/bounce instead — faceless is the strongest differentiator.
- **Accessory ideas (original):** a tiny **propeller beanie** or **single antenna-with-ball** on the dome; a **number bib** (racer identity); **sneaker-style feet** (color-blocked toe caps); an optional **backpack bud** that bounces physically. Keep accessories as separate swappable slots for cosmetics.
- **Material:** single vinyl/plastic shader from §3 (roughness 0.2, slight subsurface tint) so the whole character reads as one toy; rim-light the silhouette with INK (`#2B2D42`) at ~2 px for cartoon readability against bright backgrounds.

---

### Verification & remaining uncertainty
- **Verified by direct fetch:** all GitHub permalinks (SHAs `e1eeec22…` for james-truong, `1339106e…` for LeeHaEun1) and all Wikipedia article URLs. Tuning numbers (sweeper 150°/s, platform 1 m/s over 1 m, piston 0.5 m/s + 2 s dwell, bumper bounciness default 0.2, player 5 m/s / jump 5) are quoted from the cited source lines.
- **Labeled inference (not from a fetched source):** the §1 pacing/density/checkpoint numbers, sweeper clear-heights, bridge-width ratio, §3 palette construction rules, §4 stopwatch format & HUD layout, and the entirety of §5 character proportions — these are design recommendations derived from the cited principles and the verified player physics, and should be validated by playtesting.
- **Not retrieved this turn (flagged):** specific GDC Level Design Workshop transcripts and Game Developer long-form articles (fetch buffer limit / login wall). If you need a quoted GDC citation, that retrieval requires a different tool path and should be treated as outstanding.
